source.title: The 5 Love Languages
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of The 5 Love Languages by Gary Chapman (1992). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: People feel loved in different ways
cards.body:
Chapman's core idea is that people tend to express and recognise love through one main channel. He names five: kind words, focused time together, gifts, helpful actions and physical touch.

Problems arise when two people speak different languages. One partner may work hard to help around the house while the other mostly longs for undivided attention, and both end up feeling unappreciated. Learning which way your partner best receives love lets your effort land where it counts.
cards.apply_it: Ask someone close to you which of the five makes them feel most cared for, and share your own.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of Chapman's five love languages?
quiz.explanation: The five are words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service and physical touch.

cards.title: Keep the emotional 'love tank' topped up
cards.body:
Chapman uses the picture of an emotional tank. When it's full, people feel secure and can handle stress and disagreement more generously. When it's empty, small issues turn into big fights and partners feel distant.

The tank is filled most efficiently by love expressed in the person's main language. That means a regular, small habit of speaking their language often does more than an occasional grand gesture in a language they don't value.
cards.apply_it: Plan one small action in your partner's or friend's love language for each day this week.

quiz.question: What does Chapman's 'love tank' image suggest?
options: People cope better when they regularly feel loved in their own language
Love is limited and runs out for good
It matters only early in a relationship
quiz.explanation: A full tank makes people more secure; filling it in their language works best.

cards.title: Find someone's love language by noticing their complaints and requests
cards.body:
Chapman suggests a few clues for working out a person's primary language. Look at what they most often ask for, what they complain about when hurt, and how they tend to show love to others.

A frequent complaint like 'we never spend time together' points to quality time, while 'you never notice what I do' may point to words of affirmation. Complaints that feel annoying can actually be useful directions to what the person needs most.
cards.apply_it: Write down the last two complaints or requests someone close to you made. What love language might they point to?

quiz.question: Which clue does Chapman suggest for discovering someone's love language?
options: What they complain about and ask for most
quiz.explanation: Repeated complaints and requests often reveal the unmet need.

cards.title: When the early spark fades, love becomes a choice
cards.body:
Chapman describes the excited, obsessive phase of falling in love as real but temporary. When it fades, many couples think something is wrong.

His view is that a deeper kind of love begins here: a deliberate decision to care for the other person, including speaking their language when it doesn't come naturally. Feelings often follow actions, so choosing to love in practical ways can renew warmth that seemed lost.
cards.apply_it: Choose one loving action this week that doesn't come naturally to you, and do it without expecting anything back.

quiz.question: What happens after the 'in love' phase, according to Chapman?
options: Lasting love relies more on deliberate choices
quiz.explanation: He sees mature love as a choice expressed through actions, not just a feeling.

cards.title: Within each language, the details matter
cards.body:
Chapman notes that each love language has 'dialects'. Quality time, for example, isn't just being in the same room; it means undivided attention, such as a real conversation with phones away. Gifts don't need to be expensive; what counts is the thought they show.

So knowing someone's language is only the start. Paying attention to the specific forms that matter to them, like the kind of words, time or help they value, makes your effort truly felt.
cards.apply_it: For someone close to you, write one very specific version of their love language, such as a 20-minute walk with no phones.

quiz.question: According to Chapman, what does real quality time involve?
quiz.explanation: Being nearby isn't enough; focused attention is what makes time together count.
